A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIMIC-ILS dataset and ROSALIA model. All 23 pages of each version, including appendices A–G, are readable, and corresponding text, equations, tables, and figures can be reliably matched.

before.justification: V1 reports original segmentation and text-response experiments, qualitative predictions, and a four-physician assessment of generated annotations in Tables 3–6 and the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains these original results and adds pipeline-recall, threshold-sensitivity, and paraphrased-instruction experiments in Appendices A.7 and C.3.

M1.justification: The mask-generation pipeline, Algorithm 1, LISA-based architecture, losses, and inference procedure remain unchanged. Figure 9 removes an extra output field inconsistent with the six-field extraction already specified in v1; this corrects documentation rather than establishing a changed underlying method.

E1.justification: Appendix C.3 adds training and evaluation with generated instruction paraphrases representing medical experts, laypersons, and AI developers, extending linguistic input conditions. The underlying CXR data, seven lesion categories, and segmentation tasks remain unchanged; no actual new user population is studied.

E2.justification: Table 4 and the qualitative comparisons retain LISA-7B/13B, Text4Seg, PixelLM-7B/13B, BiomedParse, RecLMIS, and IMIS-Net. The added LISA experiments vary training data rather than introduce external comparators; Qwen3 serves as a paraphrase generator.

E3.justification: V2 adds default-versus-halved threshold evaluation with pipeline recall, downstream training on higher-recall data, and training/testing with nine paraphrases per original instruction. These are additional experimental settings; the original splits, training configuration, and benchmark evaluation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.7 adds a focused threshold-sensitivity analysis linking retained-sample recall to downstream performance. Appendix C.3 adds a linguistic-diversity check using paraphrased training and test instructions. Existing qualitative analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or comparable uncertainty estimates. The added experiments continue reporting single values.

E6.justification: Existing numerical results remain unchanged. New Table 8 reports average recall of 28.3 for default thresholds and 47.3 for halved thresholds. A.7 adds higher-recall training results of 54.3/61.4/95.8, and C.3 adds paraphrased-training/test results of 67.3/73.1/96.5, ordered as gIoU/cIoU/N-Acc percentages. These are additional settings, not revised original scores.

T1.justification: The anomaly-map definition, mask-selection conditions, Algorithm 1, and loss equations are unchanged. V2 introduces no new formal assumptions, derivations, theorems, or proofs; pipeline recall is reported empirically without a new mathematical treatment.

C1.justification: The abstract narrows the novelty framing from a new paradigm to a medical-domain adaptation of referring image segmentation. ROSALIA is more explicitly presented as fine-tuned LISA. The central contributions—automated dataset construction, MIMIC-ILS, and demonstrated segmentation utility—remain intact.

C2.justification: A.7 adds a rationale for prioritizing high-confidence masks over pipeline recall. C.3 argues that disease–anatomy combinations provide functional diversity and explains potential layperson use through global and repeated location queries. These usability interpretations are not supported by an added user study.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the future-release promise with a stated dataset/model release and repository link. It identifies Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and the nine-variant paraphrasing procedure, and corrects Figure 9's extraction schema. Existing hardware and training details are retained.

R1.justification: V2 explicitly positions ILS within referring image segmentation and foregrounds ROSALIA's dependence on LISA, which v1 already acknowledged in its method sections. The bibliography retains the same 48 cited works.

P1.justification: Targeted abstract, introduction, and conclusion edits refine terminology and attribution; Section 2.2 is renamed. Two appendix subsections and acknowledgments are added, with corresponding contents updates. The overall narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: V2 adds the recall comparison as Table 8 and renumbers subsequent appendix tables. Small prompt and label edits occur in Figures 6, 9, and 11, alongside local text and reference reflow. Existing diagrams and qualitative images are retained.

improvement.justification: Relative to v1, clearer RIS/LISA attribution, corrected prompt documentation, and the new threshold and paraphrase checks modestly improve clarity, reproducibility, and empirical support. The main results remain unchanged. The added layperson-usability argument lacks a user study, limiting the strength of the clinical implications.
